He promised that if the monster had not shown itself within three days, he would turn the ship round and set her course for New York, and no man could blame him. A faint cheer went up, but it was the cheer of men who were glad to be going home.

Twice in those last days a lookout shouted that he had found the creature, and twice the whole ship rushed towards what proved to be nothing more than a harmless whale. Each failure made the crew a little sadder, and each failure made Ned Land laugh a little louder. By the evening of the third day almost no one expected anything but a calm return.

On the third night the sea lay flat as glass beneath a sky crowded with stars, and the watch was nearly over when a shout came from the bow. A long pale light had appeared on the surface a short distance away, glowing steadily from somewhere beneath the waves. Aronnax felt his heart beat faster, for he knew that nothing in nature gave off a light of that kind.

Farragut ordered full steam, and the frigate leaped forward with her engines roaring and her whole frame trembling like a living thing. The creature kept ahead of her with ease, rising and sinking, as if it were amusing itself at the expense of a clumsy rival. Aronnax watched the glow with deep fascination, and under it he felt the first cold stirrings of fear.

Ned Land stood at the bow with his harpoon raised and his eyes fixed on the water, calm as a man who has done the same thing a thousand times. At the right moment he hurled the weapon with all the force of his great arm, but the point rang against the creature's hide as if it had struck a plate of iron. Aronnax noticed, with a puzzled mind, that the beast seemed to be neither hurt nor angry at all.

The light suddenly went out, and the sea around the frigate became black and silent, as though the monster had never existed. For hours the crew waited with the guns loaded and their eyes straining at the darkness, and nobody dared to speak above a whisper. Aronnax leaned on the rail and felt that something terrible was about to happen.

Without any warning a tremendous force struck the frigate from below and shook her from stem to stern, and the deck rose and fell like the floor in an earthquake. Aronnax was thrown over the rail like a toy, and the dark sea closed over his head. He sank deep into the cold, and the roaring of the water was the last sound he knew.

His heavy clothes dragged him down like lead, and for some moments he fought desperately for air in the blackness of the sea. Then a strong hand seized his collar and pulled him up, and he knew the loyal hand of Conseil, who had leaped in after his master without a moment's thought. Close by, Ned Land was swimming towards them as the lights of the frigate drifted away.

The three castaways crawled out of the water and found beneath their hands a long, smooth back, curved like the hull of a ship and still faintly warm. Ned Land knocked upon it with his knuckles and announced, in a voice full of both triumph and anger, that the monster was made of iron. Aronnax could hardly believe him, and yet in the pale light of dawn the truth was suddenly beyond all doubt.

They sat huddled together upon the metal back while the creature carried them across the dark sea with scarcely any noise at all. Aronnax felt cold, weak and bewildered, for he had spent his life studying animals, and now he found himself riding upon a machine. The stars wheeled slowly overhead, and the hours of that long night seemed to him almost endless.

As dawn came the creature began to move more swiftly, and the three men could scarcely keep their hold upon its slippery back. They shouted with all their strength and beat upon the metal with their fists, and at last a round door opened in the hull. Ned Land cried out in joy at the sight of the sky, but his joy did not last for very long.

Strong hands, belonging to men whose faces were hidden by masks, seized the prisoners and dragged them down a narrow ladder into the vessel. The heavy door closed above them with a clang, and they were left in a darkness so thick that Aronnax could not see his own hand. He heard Conseil breathing steadily beside him and, farther off, Ned Land muttering with rage against the whole world.

The cell had no window, no furniture and no light, and the three men searched it with their hands, finding nothing but cold iron walls. Hunger and thirst soon added themselves to their fear, and Ned Land, whose temper was already short, kicked at the door until his foot ached. Aronnax tried to think calmly, but he could find no explanation for what had happened.

At last a soft light flooded the cell, and a silent steward entered with dry clothes and a plentiful meal, which was served on plates of the finest metal. Each plate, each fork and each spoon was marked with a single letter N and a motto in Latin, and the three hungry men ate in silence. Aronnax studied the mark carefully while he ate, for it seemed to him the first small clue to a very great mystery.

The door opened again, and a tall man with piercing dark eyes and a proud, pale face stood in the doorway, so still that he might have been carved from stone. He spoke in perfect French and said calmly that his name was Captain Nemo and that he was the master of the vessel. Aronnax rose to his feet at once, unable for a long moment to say a single word.

Nemo told his guest that he had read his book on the mysteries of the deep sea and that he valued it above every other work on the subject. Aronnax was surprised and, in spite of everything, flattered, for it is a strange feeling to be praised by a jailer. He noticed, however, that the captain's perfect courtesy hid a deep and settled sadness that nothing could cure.

Nemo went on to say that he had long ago broken with the world of men and all its laws, and that the secret of his ship must be kept at any price. For this reason, he declared, none of the three could ever be allowed to leave, though he promised that they would be treated as guests and not as prisoners. His voice was gentle and almost kind, but his sentence was as final as a door closing for ever.

Ned Land leaped up and shouted that no man on earth had the right to keep honest people prisoner, and he used several words that would have made a sailor blush. Nemo heard him out with perfect calm, bowed slightly, and left the room as if the matter had already been decided long before. Aronnax understood then, with a sinking heart, that no argument of theirs would ever move this strange and secret man.

On the next morning the three men were given a breakfast of fish, shellfish and delicate sea plants, and Aronnax was astonished to find it delicious. He soon learned that his new clothes were woven from a fine silk made by sea creatures, and that nearly everything aboard the ship, from the food to the paper, had been taken from the ocean. It seemed that Captain Nemo needed nothing at all from the land, and wanted nothing from it either.

Nemo led his guest into a long and quiet library, where twelve thousand volumes in half a dozen languages stood in handsome rows. He said that the professor might read any of them whenever he pleased, though Aronnax noticed with surprise that there was not a single book on politics or on money. It was as if the captain had removed from his shelves everything that belonged to the quarrels of men, and he wished only to live among the quiet things of the mind.

The great salon was as splendid as the hall of a palace, with famous paintings upon the walls, statues in the corners and a soft light falling from the ceiling. In the centre, in glass cases, lay a museum of shells, corals and strange creatures, each one carefully labelled in the neat hand of a scientist. Aronnax walked slowly round the room, lost in wonder, and Conseil followed him with his mouth open.

Most wonderful of all were the pearls, which glowed in their cases with a soft light that no jeweller could imitate. Some were pink, some were black and some were as large as the egg of a small bird, and Aronnax knew that the sum of their value would have bought a kingdom. Nemo watched the professor's face with a faint smile, like a man who has waited a long time for someone to understand.

In the evening Nemo sat down at the great organ in the salon and played for an hour without a word of explanation. The music rose and fell like the sea itself, grave and tender and full of sorrow, and the three prisoners sat still as stone. Aronnax felt that the captain was trying to drown some old pain in the sound.

On the following day Nemo took his guest down to the engine room, which was bright and clean and almost entirely silent. There was no furnace, no smoke and no steam, and the captain explained with quiet pride that all the power of the ship came from electricity, which drove the engines, lit the lamps and warmed the rooms. Aronnax, who had studied science all his life, found it hard to believe that a vessel so simple could be so mighty.

Nemo went on to explain that his batteries were fed with sodium, which he took from the sea water that flowed around the hull. Since the ocean would never run dry, the Nautilus could sail for months without once having to seek a port or a supply of fuel. Aronnax realised that the captain had solved a problem which the greatest engineers in Europe had never yet been able to touch.

The Nautilus was shaped like an enormous cigar, about seventy metres in length, and she was built with two strong hulls, one inside the other, so that she could resist the weight of the deepest water. At her front was a sharp steel ram, which could cut open the side of any ship that came in her way. Aronnax suddenly understood, with a shiver, how the great monster had wounded so many vessels in so many seas.

When Nemo wished to dive, his men opened the valves and filled great tanks with sea water, and the whole ship grew slowly heavy. Aronnax felt the floor tilt gently under his feet, and a few moments later the waves closed over the windows of the salon and the light turned from gold to green. Not a sound or a shudder told him that he had left the surface of the world.

Nemo pressed a button, and two great steel shutters slid back from the thick glass to reveal the open sea. The three prisoners drew close to the window, and a procession of fish of every shape and colour passed through the shining blue water, as if for the sole pleasure of the guests. Conseil, who loved nothing so much as a classification, named them one after another in a low and happy voice.

Aronnax slowly settled into his strange new existence beneath the waves, and the days took on a regular rhythm. He spent his mornings in the library and his afternoons in the great salon, where he filled notebook after notebook with all that passed behind the windows. He had never been so happy as a scientist, and he had never been so unhappy as a man.

Ned Land counted the days of his captivity by making marks on the wall of his cabin with a nail, and the number of marks grew with every week. He complained to anyone who would listen that he was losing his mind, and he swore that each hour on the ship was an hour stolen from his life. Aronnax felt sorry for him and understood him perfectly, for he too longed for the shore and for the world.

At noon each day Captain Nemo climbed to the top of the ship and measured the height of the sun with a brass instrument, as seriously as a priest at his duty. He wrote down the position of the Nautilus in a small book, but he never once told the professor where they were. Aronnax realised that he was meant to be a guest without a map, and a traveller who must never learn the way.

For many days the Nautilus followed a warm current that flows north and east from the coast of Japan across the great ocean. The Japanese call it the Black Current, because its deep blue water looks almost dark against the surrounding sea, and Aronnax studied its colour with delight. He noted that its temperature rose and fell with the depth, and that its fish were not the fish of the cold waters nearby.

One night the Nautilus rose to the surface, and Nemo allowed Aronnax to step out onto the narrow deck and breathe the open air. The night was cool and sweet, the stars were brilliant, and the wind carried the smell of salt and distant land. The professor stood motionless for a long time, afraid that if he moved the freedom would vanish.

Nemo showed Aronnax a small boat that lay fixed in a hollow of the hull, so smoothly fitted that no one could have guessed it was there. It could be launched in a few moments and would carry eight people across the surface of the sea, and the captain used it, he said, when he wished to visit the coast. Ned Land, who happened to be present, looked at the little boat with burning eyes, and said nothing at all.

One evening, as they stood together at the great window, Nemo told his guest that the sea was the only place in the world where a man could be truly free. No tyrant had power upon its waters, he said, and there nobody could be made to obey a cruel law, or forced to bend before another man's will. His voice trembled slightly, and Aronnax understood that he was speaking of his own past.

Conseil told his master calmly that the sea was an excellent place to study, and that he had never seen so many species in the whole of his life. Ned Land growled that he would rather see one green field than a thousand fish, and that Conseil's patience made him want to shout. Aronnax smiled at them both, for their differences were beginning to seem like a family's.

On the table in Aronnax's cabin there lay the next morning a short note written in a neat and elegant hand. It invited the professor and his two friends to join Captain Nemo in a hunt in the forests of Crespo Island, which the captain declared to be his own. Aronnax read it twice, for it seemed impossible that anyone could own a forest at the bottom of the sea.

Ned Land was delighted by the invitation, for any change was welcome to a man who had spent weeks in an iron prison, and he dreamed already of fresh game for his dinner. Conseil agreed to go with them, as he would have gone anywhere his master went, and the two of them asked a hundred questions about the hunt. Aronnax could not answer one of them, but he felt a thrill of curiosity.

In a small chamber near the front of the ship the three guests were helped into heavy suits of rubber and copper helmets with round glass windows, and each was given a lamp and a tank of air. Nemo then showed them a pair of strange guns, which fired small glass balls charged with electricity and killed at a distance without any noise. Ned Land took his gun as tenderly as if it were a gift from a king.

The four men stepped together into a narrow chamber, and the heavy door closed behind them with a muffled sound. Sea water poured in around their legs and rose to their shoulders and over their helmets, and then a second door swung open to show them the dark ocean. Aronnax took a deep breath of the cold, dry air in his helmet and walked out into the sea.

They moved out onto a wide plain of fine sand that stretched away into the blue, and each step raised a small cloud that settled slowly behind them. The sunlight had faded to a soft green glow, and all around them the world was strangely still, like a landscape from a dream. Aronnax was astonished to find that it was so easy to walk with the weight of the sea above him.

Aronnax could not speak inside his helmet, and neither could Conseil, so the two friends made signs to each other and pointed at everything that passed. A fish drifted close to the professor's face, and a shell the size of a dinner plate lay shining at his feet like a jewel. He found himself laughing in silence, with a joy he had not felt since boyhood.

Ahead of them rose a great forest of tall plants, which swayed softly in the current like trees in a gentle wind, though no wind had ever touched them. Their branches wove together overhead and shut out most of the light, and the hunters were forced to turn on their lamps. Aronnax thought that it was the strangest wood in all the world, and certainly the most silent.

Nemo and Ned Land walked on ahead with their guns ready, hunting among the long weeds as quietly as shadows. Nemo brought down a sea otter with a single shot, and the animal drifted slowly to the sand with its fur rippling in the water. Ned Land looked at his gun with real respect, as though he had suddenly become a believer.

Suddenly a large bird passed low over the water far above the forest, and Ned Land raised his gun and fired, and the bird fell as slowly as a leaf in autumn. The harpooner lifted it from the sand with a broad smile, and for a moment he was as happy as he had ever been aboard the ship. Aronnax saw that the hunt had given him something that the long weeks of captivity had taken away.

After several hours of walking, Nemo raised his hand and signalled that it was time to rest, and the four men lay down on a soft bed of sand beneath the shelter of the plants. The silence there was so profound that Aronnax could hear his own heart, and before long a heavy sleep came over him. His last thought was of the great weight of water above him, which seemed as gentle as a blanket.

When the travellers woke, the light above them was dim and blue, for the sun was sinking far overhead on the surface of the world. Nemo led the party back across the plain without once looking behind him, and their four lamps made small circles of gold on the darkening sand. Aronnax followed in a kind of trance, aware that he would remember this walk until the end of his life.

The Nautilus waited for them in the dark with every window glowing, like a house seen from the road on a winter night. Back in the salon, Aronnax sat down quietly and said little, for he had suddenly understood that Captain Nemo had built for himself an entire world beneath the waves. It was a world with its own forests, its own laws and its own loneliness, and nobody else on earth had ever been admitted to it.

For many days the Nautilus travelled across the Pacific, covering thousands of leagues and passing group after group of low islands ringed with coral. Aronnax counted them from the window of the salon, and he marvelled that a distance which a sailing ship needed months to cross could be covered in a few weeks. The ocean seemed to him endless, and yet, to his own surprise, it had begun to feel strangely like a home.

Day after day Aronnax and Conseil filled their notebooks with fish that no naturalist had ever described, and the salon windows were the finest laboratory in the world. Conseil sorted each creature into its proper family with calm precision, and the professor was amazed that his modest servant had so many names in his head. Together they began to feel that they were working on a book that nobody else could ever write.

Ned Land often stood in silence before the small boat in the hollow of the hull, and Aronnax could guess what thoughts filled his mind. The professor begged the Canadian to be patient and warned him that an escape which failed would cost all three of them their lives. Ned said nothing in reply, but his jaw was set like a stone, and Aronnax knew that the matter was far from finished.

One day the sea above the Nautilus was torn by a terrible storm, with waves as tall as houses and a wind that tore the tops from the swell. Nemo had the ship sink a little deeper, and within a few moments the three guests were gliding through water as calm and clear as a garden pond. Aronnax realised that for this captain no storm on the surface could ever be a real danger to his ship.

As the Nautilus approached the western Pacific, Aronnax remembered the story of La Pérouse, the French explorer who had sailed from France in 1785 in command of two ships on a voyage of discovery. In 1788 he sent a last letter from Australia, and after that he and all his men vanished without a trace. For nearly forty years nobody could say what had become of them, and the whole of France wondered and grieved.

At last the Nautilus came to the island of Vanikoro, which is ringed by a deadly reef of coral, and the professor knew at once where he was. The two ships of La Pérouse had been wrecked upon this reef, and Aronnax's heart beat faster as the Nautilus slid slowly along the edge of the dark water. He pressed his face against the glass and held his breath, as though the silent wreck might still speak to him.

Through the great window he could see an old anchor lying half buried in the coral, and near it a rusty cannon and some lumps of lead that had been green with weed for years. They were all that remained of the proud ships, and they had lain in the silence of the sea for nearly eighty years. Aronnax felt a strange and heavy sadness, as though he were looking down upon a grave that no one had ever marked.

Nemo stood at the window with his head uncovered, a thing the professor had never seen him do, and for a long time he did not speak. At last he said quietly that he had come to this place before and that the sea kept more secrets than any man could ever learn. Aronnax wondered, in the quiet that followed, what secrets the captain himself was hiding behind that proud and silent face.

Aronnax told his two friends what he knew of the history of the lost ships, and how a captain named Dillon had found pieces of the wreck in 1826. He added that a French expedition had later raised a stone monument upon the shore to the memory of the lost sailors, so that their names would never be forgotten. Conseil listened with bowed head, as if he were standing at a funeral, and even Ned Land stopped grumbling for a while.

As the sun went down behind the reef, the Nautilus turned away from the lonely island and set her course to the west, towards the dangerous waters of the Torres Strait. Nemo spoke no more that evening, and he did not take his place at the organ. Aronnax thought that the visit to the wreck had left the captain sadder than he had been before, and he did not know why.

The Nautilus entered the Torres Strait, that narrow channel between Australia and New Guinea, which is full of reefs and shallow banks and has been the grave of many ships. Aronnax stood at the window and watched the coral pass beneath them in long ridges, bright and sharp as knives. He knew that a single mistake would end the voyage and perhaps their lives.

Nemo took the wheel himself, an act which the professor had never seen, and steered the ship through the dangerous passage with perfect steadiness. The crew worked in complete silence, and the lamp in the small room made the captain's face look as pale as marble. Aronnax realised that even this proud man was afraid of the sea in this place.

In the middle of the night there was a sudden shock, followed by a long and terrible grinding sound, and the Nautilus stopped as if a giant hand had seized her. She had run onto a bank of coral that was not marked on any chart, and she could not move. Aronnax rose from his bed and hurried to the salon, where he found Nemo standing quite calmly.

The captain studied his tables and told Aronnax that there was no danger and no cause for alarm. He explained that the tide in these waters would rise in four days to a height which would lift the ship from the bank without damage, and that nothing remained but to wait. Aronnax marvelled at his composure, for any other captain would have been pale with terror.

Ned Land could not hide his joy, for across the water he could see the green shore of an island that was no more than a few miles away. He asked the captain, with a politeness that was rare in him, whether the three of them might go ashore to hunt, and he promised faithfully that they would return. The professor suspected that Ned was already dreaming of leaving them for good, and he said nothing.

To everyone's surprise Nemo gave his consent at once, and he even ordered the small boat to be made ready. He only warned them to be careful, because the people of that coast were fierce and unfriendly to strangers, and he reminded them that the Nautilus would not wait for ever. Ned Land thanked him with a glance that was almost friendly, and then hurried down to the small boat.

The boat reached the beach in less than an hour, and Ned Land leaped onto the sand, fell on his knees and kissed the warm ground like a sailor returning from a long exile. Conseil laughed aloud at the sight of him, and even the grave professor could not help smiling. After weeks beneath the sea, the touch of solid earth was like a draught of wine.

The island was covered with tall coconut palms and other fruit trees, and the three men gathered a mountain of food in a matter of minutes. They drank the sweet milk of the nuts and ate until they could hold no more, and they declared the meal finer than any they had eaten in the grandest of hotels. It was, Aronnax thought, the simplest happiness in the world, and he had not known how much he had missed it.

Ned Land went off into the forest with his gun and soon returned with half a dozen wild pigeons, which Conseil roasted over a fire on the beach with the skill of a chef. The three friends ate the birds in the shade of the palms, and for a few hours they forgot that they were prisoners. Ned in particular looked like a man made new again, with his cheeks red and his broad shoulders at ease.

As the sun began to sink, Aronnax noticed a footprint in the damp sand at the edge of the forest, and a few steps further on he found a broken branch. He remembered the captain's warning about the people of that coast, and a chill ran through his body. The forest, which a moment before had seemed so peaceful, now seemed full of watching eyes.

Aronnax told his friends what he had seen, and the three men gathered their baskets of fruit and set off at a quick pace across the sand towards the boat. Ned Land kept his gun ready, and Conseil looked anxiously over his shoulder, but the forest seemed quiet and empty. Aronnax could not shake off the uneasy feeling that they were being watched by unseen eyes among the trees.

Before they could reach the water, a crowd of islanders came bursting out of the trees with spears, bows and slings, shouting in a loud and angry tone. They were so many that the three men saw at a glance that to fight would have been madness. Ned Land swore and ran, and for once the professor was glad that he had a sailor's legs.

The friends dragged the boat into the sea and rowed with all their strength while stones fell and splashed on every side. One of them struck the side of the little craft with a sharp crack, but nobody was hurt, and the shore slowly shrank behind them. Aronnax looked back and saw a line of dark figures standing on the sand, shaking their fists.

The three men reached the Nautilus out of breath, climbed upon her back and hurried down the hatch, and Nemo met them in the salon with a face that showed neither anger nor surprise. He said quietly that it was fortunate they had come back in time, and he asked no questions about their adventure. Aronnax felt that the captain knew a great deal more than he was willing to say, and that he had been waiting for them.

At sunrise the sea around the Nautilus was covered with canoes, and in them sat hundreds of islanders, their faces painted and their eyes wide with curiosity and greed. Aronnax counted them through the window until he lost count, and he realised that the island had sent every man it could find against the iron whale. Ned Land, who was standing beside him with his gun in his hand, had turned very pale beneath his weathered skin.

The islanders climbed onto the deck of the ship and began to pound upon the hatch with clubs and stones, and the noise inside the Nautilus was like the beating of a great drum. The crew listened and waited without a word, and Nemo looked at the clock as calmly as if nothing were wrong. Aronnax found the perfect silence of the crew a good deal more alarming than all the noise that was going on outside.

Nemo gave a short order, and at once a powerful electric current ran through the iron rails on the deck. Every islander who touched them gave a loud cry and fell back, and in a few moments the whole crowd was running for the canoes, shaking their arms in terror. Never in their lives had they felt such a force, and they believed that a god had struck them.

Aronnax asked the captain with some anxiety whether anyone had been killed, and Nemo answered that nobody had been seriously hurt. He had meant only to defend his ship, he said, and the islanders would soon forget the shock and tell stories of it round their fires. The professor was relieved, and it was the first time he had seen the captain's mercy.

At two in the afternoon the tide reached its height, exactly as Nemo had said it would, and the Nautilus rose gently from the bank of coral. Her engines started with a deep hum, and she glided back into the open water as if nothing had ever hindered her. Aronnax admired the captain's calm, for in all those anxious days he had not doubted his tide for a single moment.

The Nautilus dived beneath the waves and slipped out through the Torres Strait, leaving the island and its forests far behind. Ned Land sat alone in his cabin and did not speak to anyone, for the chance that he had hoped for had passed. Aronnax pitied him, but he knew that the harpooner would not give up easily.

The Nautilus left the Torres Strait behind and passed out into the open sea, and the long, quiet hours resumed their flow. Aronnax could not sleep, and as he lay in his narrow cabin his mind went back across the oceans to his home and to everything that he had lost. Conseil's regular breathing in the next room was the only thing that comforted him.

Late one night there was a knock at the professor's door, and Nemo appeared, pale and troubled, with a lamp in his hand. One of his men had been hurt in an accident, he said, and since the professor knew something of the body, he hoped he might be able to help. It was the first time that Nemo had asked a favour from his guest.

Aronnax followed the captain to a small cabin, where a sailor lay in a bunk with a terrible wound to his head. He saw at a glance that no skill of his could save the man, and a few hours later the poor fellow died, while Nemo stood in silence at the bedside. Aronnax noticed, with surprise, that the captain's hand trembled slightly as he held the dying man's own.

On the next morning Nemo carried the body to a place which he called his cemetery, and which lay in a forest of coral not far from where the ship was resting. The whole crew went in diving suits, bearing the body in procession, and the sight of the figures moving slowly through the green water was one that Aronnax never forgot. It was a funeral in an alien world, silent and strange, where even the mourners moved like dreamers in the deep green light.

They dug a grave in the sand between the branches of pink and white coral, and the crew knelt in silence while Nemo laid upon it a small cross made of coral. Around them stood other crosses, one for each man who had died on the Nautilus, and Aronnax understood that the captain was prepared to give his friends the burial that the world above would have refused them. The service ended without a single word being spoken, and the divers rose and walked away through the coral, one behind the other.

Nemo turned to the professor and said, in a voice very different from his usual tone, that here his friend would sleep in peace, far from the sharks and from the reach of any enemy. Aronnax was deeply moved, for it was the first time he had seen so much tenderness in the captain, and he began to see that his pride was only a wall around a heart that had been wounded. He bowed his head in respect, and for a long while he could find nothing at all to say to the captain.

The Nautilus passed along the great coral reefs, where countless tiny creatures build walls and islands over the ages, and Conseil explained to Ned Land that each of them was no bigger than a pin. For once Ned Land listened without a word of complaint, and he even asked a question about the colours. Aronnax smiled at the gentle teacher and his unlikely pupil, and he thought how strange it was to find a school at the bottom of the sea.

The ship entered the Indian Ocean, and the air in the salon grew warm and heavy as the sun beat down upon the surface far overhead. Nemo asked his guest quite suddenly whether he was fond of pearls, and when Aronnax answered that he was, the captain announced that they were bound for the coast of Ceylon. A faint smile of pleasure crossed his stern face, the first that the professor had seen there for many days.

Nemo explained that the pearl fishers of Ceylon dive from small boats to a depth of about ten metres, holding their breath for as long as they can and bringing up as many oysters as they can carry. Their work was hard and dangerous, he said, because the sharks of those waters waited for them and took more than one diver every year. His voice had a bitter edge, as though he were speaking of some old injustice that he could not forgive or forget.

The Nautilus sank to the bottom in the Gulf of Manaar and rested on a rocky bed which was covered with pearl oysters as far as the lamps could shine. Aronnax stood at the window and gazed in amazement, for he had never imagined that the sea could hold so many, packed together like stones in a pavement. Each of those plain grey shells, he knew, might hide a treasure fit for the crown of a king, and nobody would ever guess it.

On the following day Nemo, Aronnax, Conseil and Ned Land put on their diving suits and walked out in a line across the sea floor, among beds of pearl oysters that lay in rows upon the rocks. Some of the shells were as large as dinner plates, and their rough grey surfaces gave no hint of the treasure they might hold. The captain led the way as calmly as a gardener in his own orchard.

Nemo opened one of the shells with a quick turn of his knife and showed the professor a small, shining pearl nestled inside. He explained by signs that a pearl begins as a tiny grain of sand which hurts the animal, and which the animal covers over with layer after layer of smooth material, year after year. Then he carefully set the oyster back in its place, so that the little creature might go on with its quiet work.

The captain led his friends to a deep cave in the rock, in the middle of which lay an immense shell resting open on the sand, its edges covered with long green weeds. It was wider than a table, and it was so heavy that a man could not have lifted it, and Aronnax understood that he was looking at the greatest of all the shell-bearing creatures. He moved closer to the open shell, with his heart beating hard against his ribs and his eyes wide behind the glass.

Inside the giant shell lay a perfect white pearl as large as a coconut, as round as a ball and shining with a soft and mysterious light. Aronnax reckoned that it must be worth at least ten million francs, and he hardly dared to breathe in case the sight should disappear. Conseil, who was standing at his side with both hands raised, seemed to have lost his power of speech for a while.

By signs Nemo told the professor that he came to look at the pearl every year and that he let it grow a little more, like a child. He had no desire to take it from its bed, he indicated, because in the sea it was more beautiful than it could ever be in any crown. Aronnax understood, as he watched him, that this was a captain who valued beauty far more than he valued any riches.

On the following day the friends returned to the banks and saw an Indian diver sinking from a boat above them, with a stone tied to his foot and a basket on his arm. The man was thin and dark, and he went quickly to work, picking oysters from the rocks and dropping them into the basket without raising his eyes. He had no idea that anyone was watching him from below, or that his life was soon to hang by a thread.

Suddenly a great grey shadow rose from the deep behind the diver, and Aronnax saw with horror a huge shark with its jaws wide open and its rows of white teeth shining in the dim light. The man, who was busy at his work, did not turn around, and the monster glided towards him with slow and terrible ease. For a moment time seemed to stop, and the professor could hear nothing in his helmet but the beating of his own heart.

Nemo flung himself between the diver and the shark with a long dagger in his hand and met the beast with all the force of his body. The shark struck at him and knocked him to the ground, and its great jaws opened above his head like the doors of a tomb. Aronnax could not move a muscle, and in his mind he cried out in despair for the brave and strange man on the sand.

At that instant Ned Land darted forward with his harpoon and drove it deep into the shark's side with a single mighty thrust. The beast shuddered, thrashed once, and sank to the sand, dead, while Nemo rose unhurt from the ground. The three friends carried the unconscious diver up from the sea floor and into the daylight.

When the man opened his eyes on the surface, Nemo put into his hands a heavy bag of pearls, and the diver stared at it as though he were dreaming. Aronnax watched in silence, for he now understood that behind the captain's cold words lay a heart that could give without asking. He thought that a man who gave so freely could not be wholly bad.

The Nautilus left the coast of Ceylon behind and sailed north and west across the hot Arabian Sea, her white wake smoothing out behind her. Nemo did not say where she was bound, but the professor could read the position on the charts, and he knew that the Red Sea lay ahead. For several days the life aboard went on in its quiet and orderly manner.

The ship entered the Red Sea, that long narrow arm of water between Africa and Arabia, which is bordered on both sides by dry and golden hills. Aronnax studied its fish and its corals with great interest, and he learned that its famous colour comes from countless tiny red plants that float upon the surface. Conseil wrote down every name in his notebook with his usual patience, and sorted the fishes into their proper families.

Aronnax asked the captain how the Nautilus could possibly pass into the Mediterranean, since the isthmus of Suez stood in her way like a wall of sand. The canal which was to cut through it was not yet finished, he reminded him, and the ship was far too large to be dragged across the desert. Nemo listened to all of these objections with an expression of quiet amusement, and let the professor finish.

The captain smiled and replied that there was a secret passage, which he had discovered himself and which he called the Arabian Tunnel, and that it ran beneath the sands from sea to sea. The Nautilus approached the town of Suez on the following night, and then she dived to the mouth of the tunnel in the dark. Aronnax could not tell, as the great ship sank into the black water, whether he was awake or dreaming.

The ship raced through the narrow tunnel in the dark, borne along like a leaf on a rapid current, and the pale walls of rock flashed past the windows in a blur. The professor held his breath and counted the seconds, and in a very short time the Nautilus had passed beneath the whole width of the isthmus. He could scarcely believe that so great a journey had been made so easily, and under such a burning stretch of desert.

The Nautilus rose into the Mediterranean as the sun was coming up, and the water around her was a deep and sparkling blue that seemed to reach to the end of the world. Aronnax felt his heart leap in his chest, for these were the shores of the old world, the shores of Europe, of Greece and of home. He wondered what the captain felt, when he looked at them, and whether he too had ever longed for a home on those shores.

Ned Land whispered to Conseil that Europe was only a few miles away, and that this was the best chance they would ever be given. The two friends began to plan an escape in the small boat, and they decided that they would wait for a calm night and a landing on some quiet shore. Aronnax saw them talking together in low voices at the end of the salon, and without a word being said he guessed everything.

The Nautilus passed the islands of Greece so swiftly that the three men could hardly count them, and the green shores seemed to fly past the windows like pictures in a book. Ned Land stood at the glass with his fists clenched and watched them go, for he understood that the ship was moving much too fast for any escape. He gave a low groan of disappointment and turned away from the window to stare at the floor of the salon.

Aronnax would gladly have lingered in that old and glorious sea, where Homer's heroes had once sailed, and where so many cities had been built and destroyed. Nemo, however, seemed to be in a hurry, and he would not even stop to look at the ancient coasts, as if the Mediterranean held for him no pleasure at all. The professor guessed that this sea, so full of the stories of mankind, held for the captain only sad and bitter memories.

In less than two days the Nautilus crossed the entire Mediterranean from one end to the other, and she came to the narrow Strait of Gibraltar with its great rock rising out of the sea. Ned Land was bitterly angry, for every chance of leaving the ship had been lost during the voyage, and there was no use in blaming anyone. Aronnax tried to console him with a few kind words about better chances to come, but the Canadian only shook his head.

The Nautilus passed the great rock of Gibraltar and swam out of the Mediterranean into the Atlantic, whose long grey swell made her pitch gently on the surface. She turned north along the coast of Portugal, and Aronnax wondered where the captain was taking them, since Nemo had said nothing about any destination. In his heart the professor was already beginning to guess, and the guess made his pulse quicken a little.

In the dim light of Vigo Bay, off the coast of Spain, the Nautilus came to rest on the bottom, and Nemo took the professor to the window to show him what lay there. The sand was strewn with the burned wrecks of a Spanish treasure fleet that had been destroyed in battle in 1702, and the old ships lay in heaps like the bones of drowned giants. It was a grave that held a king's riches, and the Nautilus lay above it like a patient and silent watcher.

The crew walked out in their diving suits and moved across the sand with iron chests upon their shoulders and heavy bars of gold in their arms. Some of the old chests had burst open long ago, and ancient coins lay glittering on the sea floor, still bright after more than a century and a half in the water. Aronnax watched the whole scene with a mixture of wonder and discomfort, for he did not yet know what it meant.

Aronnax asked the captain what he meant to do with so much gold, and Nemo replied with a short laugh that the treasure belonged to nobody and that no one knew better than he how to use it. His tone was proud and bitter at once, and the professor understood that the money was meant for some purpose which the captain would never explain. He did not dare to ask again, for he felt that the answer would not be one that he wished to hear.

On the next day the ship followed the slope of a great mountain under the water and came out upon a broad plain, where a deep red glow from some far-off volcano lit the dark sea with a ghostly colour. Aronnax felt, without being able to say why, that he had come to a place where no human being had ever been. His heart beat strongly in his chest as the dim red light grew brighter and brighter before the ship.

Nemo and Aronnax put on their diving suits and walked together across the plain in the red light, and soon they saw the broken shapes of pillars, fallen walls and old streets, all covered with sea plants. It was the ruin of a vast city, and the silence around it was as deep as the silence of the grave. Aronnax felt as though he were walking through a dream of the distant past, among people who were long forgotten.

Nemo bent down, picked up a piece of white stone and wrote a single word upon a black rock, and the word was Atlantis. Aronnax remembered at once the story told by the Greek thinker Plato, of a great island which had sunk into the sea in a single day and night, and he felt a shiver go through him. Whether it was true, no one could say for certain, but it was a moving thought to have in such a place.

The Nautilus then visited a coal mine at the bottom of the sea, where Nemo's men worked with picks and lamps to cut the black fuel from the rock. The captain explained that his batteries needed a little of it, and that the sea, which gave him all the rest, gave him this too. Aronnax saw that Nemo had thought of everything, and that he depended upon no one in all the wide world above.

After many days the Nautilus rose into the Sargasso Sea, where a thick carpet of floating weed stretches to the horizon and slows down every ship that tries to pass. The weed lay like a golden meadow upon the water, and the Nautilus slid through it with a soft hiss, scarcely troubled by the resistance. Aronnax stood on the deck in the warm air and thought of the old sailors who had feared this strange and silent place.

Aronnax and Conseil found small fish and crabs hiding in the long yellow strands, and they noted down every kind that they saw, with great delight. Then the Nautilus dived again and turned south, towards the cold seas that lie beyond the tip of America and at the very end of the world. Aronnax felt the first breath of an adventure that no sailor had ever completed.

The Nautilus sailed south through the Atlantic, and with each day that passed the air and the water grew a little colder. The three prisoners put on thick clothes, and the sun, when it appeared at all, hung low over a heavy grey sea like a pale coin. Aronnax noted the falling temperature in his book with a scientist's pleasure and a traveller's unease.

One morning the professor saw through the window a herd of large whales swimming together close to the surface, rolling slowly in the water as if they had no fear. A pack of sperm whales, armed with their long rows of sharp teeth, dived upon them from above, and in an instant the sea was boiling with their furious fight. The noise of the water carried even through the thick glass and the double hull of the ship into the salon.

Nemo watched the scene from the window with a hard and thoughtful face and said that sperm whales were the cruellest enemies of the peaceful herd. He gave a short order to the helmsman, and the Nautilus plunged forward to take the side of the weaker animals with the stern calm of a judge. Aronnax understood that this was no impulse but a matter of principle for the captain.

The Nautilus drove into the attackers with her ram like a sword, one after another, and her sides shook with the force of each blow. In a few minutes the sea around her was stained red, and the few sperm whales that lived turned and fled with the fear of those who have met a power greater than their own. Aronnax watched in silence from the window, filled with admiration for the captain and with pity for the dying whales.

Ned Land cheered loudly in the salon, for he had never seen a ship fight like a true hunter, and he declared that he would never again doubt the captain's courage. Aronnax was thrilled, but he was also deeply saddened, for he had never been able to bear the sight of animals dying, even those that were guilty. He kept these thoughts to himself, for he did not wish to spoil the harpooner's pleasure on that cold morning.

Further south the first icebergs rose before the ship, tall and white against the dark water, and snow began to drift down on the deck like feathers. Aronnax counted twenty of them in a single hour, each one different in shape, some like castles and some like cathedrals, and the cold became so keen that it hurt to breathe. The world seemed to be turning slowly to glass, and he wondered what lay at the end of such a cold road.

Soon a high wall of ice rose across the whole horizon and stood before the Nautilus like the edge of the world, so that she could go no further on the surface. Nemo studied it for a long time in silence, and the professor wondered how he could possibly find a path through such a barrier, if indeed there was one. The ice shone coldly in the low sun, and its white face gave back no answer to his silent questions.

Aronnax and Ned Land were allowed to stand on the deck for a few minutes in the biting wind, with their coats pulled around their ears. The cold stung their faces like a thousand needles, and the silence was so deep that they could hear the ice cracking far away across the water. Ned Land muttered that he had never been so cold in all his Canadian winters.

Nemo decided to dive beneath the ice, and the Nautilus sank down into a pale blue world, lit by a strange diffused glow that came through the roof of the sea. Overhead, the vast layer of ice shone like frosted glass, and the ship moved quietly beneath it like a bird under a great tent. Aronnax felt, with a thrill that was half joy and half dread, that he had left the earth and entered another planet altogether.

At last the Nautilus rose through the water into a calm sea beyond the ice, ringed by white cliffs and pale drifting mist, and all around her the surface lay like polished steel. Penguins stood upright on the floes in rows, as solemn as little priests, and seals lifted their heads to watch the strange visitor slide by. It was a place that belonged to no nation, and perhaps to no one but the silent birds and the patient animals.

The Nautilus sailed south along narrow lanes of open water between enormous walls of ice, which rose on both sides of her like the cliffs of some drowned continent. The sun hung very low in the sky, and the whole world seemed to be made of glass, so bright and so cold that the professor could scarcely look at it. Aronnax had never in all his life seen anything so beautiful and at the same time so desolate and so cold.

One morning a bare and frozen land appeared through the mist ahead, grey and rocky, with a few black cliffs showing through the snow. Nemo announced calmly that they had come near the end of the world, and he gave orders for the small boat to be made ready. Aronnax saw that the captain's hands trembled slightly, though his voice was perfectly steady and his face showed nothing.

Nemo, Aronnax, Conseil and Ned Land took the small boat to a stony beach and walked together across the frozen ground, which rang beneath their boots like iron. Penguins and seals looked at them without the least fear, for they had never seen a man before, and they did not know that men could be dangerous. The professor felt almost guilty to disturb their peace, as though he had walked into a quiet room without knocking.

Ned Land shot a few birds and seals for fresh food, and he dragged them to the boat with a broad smile, like a boy returned from a holiday. Aronnax and Conseil meanwhile gathered mosses and pieces of rock for their collection, working quickly because of the cold, and they filled their pockets until they could carry no more. The little party seemed content for the moment, and even Ned Land forgot to talk about the day when he would escape.

Nemo sat alone on a high rock and looked south across the white land, with his hands folded and his face set like marble. He told Aronnax in a low voice that he wished to be the first human being to stand at the southern pole of the world, and that he would never rest until he had done it. The professor thought that he had never seen a man so hungry for a place.

On the next day the mist lifted for a short time, and Nemo measured the height of the sun at noon with his brass instrument, as carefully as a priest handling holy objects. He wrote down a number in his little book, and his face shone with a fierce and almost childlike joy that Aronnax had not seen before. Aronnax realised that they were standing on the very place which the captain had so long and so fiercely desired to reach.

On the top of a hill Nemo planted a black flag bearing a golden letter N, and in a loud voice he declared that he took this land for himself and for his people. The wind caught the flag and made it stream like a banner, and for a moment he looked less like a prisoner of the sea than like a king of it. Aronnax was strangely moved by the sight, and he found that he could not entirely hate the man who stood before him.

As the sun touched the edge of the horizon and began to sink, Nemo raised his arm and said farewell to it, for the long polar night was about to begin. His voice shook, and Aronnax was touched to see how deeply the captain loved the light that he had left behind him, and how much he gave up for his freedom. It was, he thought, the most human and the most touching moment that he had yet seen in the captain's long silence.

The four men rowed back to the dark ship through the drifting ice in a long and thoughtful silence, while the stars began to appear in a sky the colour of ink. Aronnax thought of the great explorers who had tried to reach this place and failed, and he was proud, in spite of himself, to have seen what they had not. He also knew, however, that he must never forget that he was still a prisoner, and that the captain's moods could change.

The Nautilus dived away from the white shore and turned her bow to the north beneath the sea, leaving the black flag behind her on its hill in the gathering dark. Overhead the long polar night was beginning, and the ice, which had been moving all that summer, was slowly growing thicker as the cold deepened. Aronnax did not yet know what that would mean for them, nor how soon the sea would test the courage of every man aboard.

In the middle of the night the Nautilus came to a sudden stop with a heavy shock, and Aronnax was flung from his bed on to the floor of his cabin. When he ran to the window of the salon he saw nothing but great walls of dark blue ice on every side, close against the glass. The ship was not moving, the engines had fallen silent, and the only sound was the groaning of the ice outside.

Nemo told him quietly that the ice had shifted during the night and had closed in behind the ship, so that the way by which they had come was gone. The Nautilus was shut up like a prisoner in a small lake, under a roof of ice that might be many feet thick, and nothing could be done by wishing. The captain spoke with the calm of a man who has met death before.

The captain looked at the gauge on the wall and said that the ship contained air for no more than two days. Nobody spoke, and Ned Land, who had been so brave in the face of sharks and spears, turned pale beneath his tan and stared at the floor. Aronnax counted the hours in his mind and found that there were not enough of them.

Nemo called his men together and ordered them to cut a way out through the ice, and they put on their diving suits and took picks and axes. They walked out upon the frozen wall with their lamps swinging in the dark, and their blows rang through the water like the strokes of a bell. Aronnax watched from the window with a strangely hopeful heart, as the white chips fell like snow upon the sea floor.

Nemo also used the engines to heat water, which he pumped, boiling, against the walls of the ice that held the ship, and a white cloud of steam rose in the freezing water. The ice melted a little at a time, with terrible slowness, and the professor realised that the captain was fighting a battle between fire and cold. He hardly dared to hope that the fire would win in the end, for the cold seemed so much stronger than the heat.

As the hours passed, the air inside the Nautilus grew heavy and warm, and the electric lamps burned low and yellow, so that the faces of the men were pale in the dimness. Aronnax felt a great weight upon his chest, and his head began to ache and swim, and every breath was a labour that tired him as a long climb would have done. Conseil sat beside him and did not complain, though his face, usually so calm, had become grey and drawn in the yellow light.

Aronnax and Ned Land joined the crew and swung their picks at the ice for hours, until their arms burned and their hands were raw. Nobody stopped, because everyone knew that to rest was to risk the lives of all, and the Canadian, who knew something of ice, worked with the strength of two men. Even Nemo took a pick, and for a while he seemed no more than one of his own sailors, tired, silent and determined.

By the end of the second day the men had cut a deep channel in the ice beneath the ship, and she began to sink slowly into it, while the walls of the ice drew close on both sides. The lamps had nearly failed, and the air was so poor that every man gasped like a fish on a river bank. Aronnax thought that the end had surely come, and he began to compose in his mind a last farewell to his friends.

Nemo gave the order for full power, and the Nautilus shot forward and upward through the narrow passage with her engines trembling, and every plate in her frame groaning as if it were alive. She struck the thin ice above her with her sharp ram, and the roof broke into pieces with a great roar, and a flood of grey light poured in upon the sea. Aronnax felt the ship leap upwards like a living creature that has finally broken free of the hunter's net.

Fresh air flooded into the ship, and the three prisoners breathed it in great gulps, like men who had been dying of thirst in the desert. Nemo thanked his tired crew in a few quiet words, and then he gave the order to turn the ship north towards warmer and kinder seas. Aronnax saw that the captain was smiling for the first time since the pole, though his face was grey with weariness.

The Nautilus sailed north from the ice, and the cold slowly faded from the water, as if the earth itself were breathing out after a long fright. The three prisoners were weak and tired, but a quiet gladness filled them, and each morning they felt a little more alive. Even Ned Land spoke to the captain with a grudging respect, because he had seen how bravely the man could fight for the lives of others.

The ship passed Cape Horn, that lonely cliff at the southern end of South America, where the wind blows hard and the seas are among the wildest in the world. Aronnax thought of all the sailors who had died there, and he was glad, for once, to be sheltered beneath the waves. The Nautilus did not even rock in the water, and the professor thought of the terrible waves above him as a story told to children.

Aronnax and Conseil spent long hours at the window studying the fish of the Atlantic along the coast of South America, and the two friends filled notebook after notebook with notes. Conseil's collection grew thicker every day, and he put every new creature into its proper family, to the professor's delight. They were as happy as two scholars shut up in a great library, and they were hardly aware of the passing of the days.

In the quiet of the library Aronnax found, to his disquiet, that he was coming to respect Captain Nemo, in spite of the iron door that kept him a prisoner. He admired the captain's learning, his courage and his gentleness to the weak, and he asked himself how such a man could also be so hard. The question had no answer that he could find, and it disturbed his sleep for many nights, like a stone in a shoe.

The Nautilus came to the mouth of the Amazon, where the water of the sea is mixed with so much fresh water that it can be tasted many miles from the shore. Aronnax filled a glass from the surface and drank it with astonishment, amazed that a single river could push so far out into the ocean. The Amazon seemed to him a sea in itself, a great moving ocean of fresh water flowing through the salt.

A great shoal of silver fish rushed past the windows in a living cloud, and soon after it a school of dolphins arrived to race the ship. They leaped and turned in the water like children at play, and Conseil laughed aloud and clapped his hands for joy. Even the stern captain watched them with a faint smile, as though they reminded him of some far-off happier time in his own life.

One evening Aronnax asked Nemo why he had left the world of men and made his home beneath the sea, and the captain answered with a sad smile. He said that the professor would hear everything one day, but he did not say when, and a shadow of pain passed over his face like a cloud over the sun. Aronnax did not dare to ask again that evening, for he felt that he had come to the edge of a wound that must not be touched.

At night the ship rose to the surface, and Aronnax stepped out on the deck under a sky blazing with stars. He found among them the old constellations of the northern sky, which he had missed for months, and he felt that he was at last near home, in spite of the iron deck beneath his feet. The thought brought tears to his eyes, and he stood there until the first grey light of morning began to show in the east.

Ned Land spoke quietly to Aronnax while Conseil kept watch at the door, and his voice was low and urgent, like that of a man planning a battle. He said that the time to escape was coming, and the professor, who had no wish to quarrel with his friend, promised that he would think about it. He did not tell Ned, however, that he was no longer certain that he wished to leave the strange man who ruled the ship.

The Nautilus turned towards the north and west, and Aronnax saw from the chart that her course pointed towards North America and the great ocean currents that flow beside it. Ned Land watched the position of the ship all day, and his hope, which had seemed to die in the ice, began to grow again. He said not a word to anyone about it, but Aronnax saw his hands close and open again and again as he stood at the window.

One afternoon a dark shape appeared at the window of the salon, and the Nautilus came to a stop in the middle of the open Atlantic, with her engines suddenly silent. Aronnax stared into the dim water and felt a cold hand close round his heart, for he had never seen anything like the shadow that pressed against the glass. Conseil, who was standing beside him with his notebook in his hand, did not breathe at all for a long moment.

It was a gigantic squid, with eight long arms covered with suckers, two huge round eyes the colour of green glass and a hard beak like a parrot's. Aronnax judged that its body was longer than a fishing boat, and he told himself that all his knowledge of nature had not prepared him for such a sight. Conseil turned pale, and Ned Land swore under his breath, as men do who see a danger that no harpoon was ever made for.

Nemo ordered the Nautilus to rise to the surface and sent his men up the stairs with axes in their hands, and his calm voice carried through the ship like a bell. Ned Land took up a harpoon and followed the crew, and Aronnax and Conseil went with him, for none of them could stay behind. The professor felt his knees shake with every step that he climbed, but he did not turn back, for he could not bear to miss the danger.

When the hatch was opened, a long grey arm pushed through the narrow gap with a horrible slow motion and felt about the stairs for something to seize. A crew member struck it with an axe, and the severed arm fell twitching on the floor like a snake, while a thick black liquid spread across the iron. The man did not even pause to look at it, for already a second arm was creeping up from the dark behind it.

On the deck the crew fought the squid, which rose from the water on every side, and a black cloud of ink spread over the sea until the waves seemed to be made of night. The air was full of waving arms, of the blows of axes and of shouts that were half cheers and half cries of fear. Aronnax, who had come on deck only to see, found himself fighting for his life with a borrowed axe in both hands.

Suddenly a huge arm seized one of the crew, lifted him high into the air as if he had been a doll and held him over the sea. The man cried out for help, and for a moment the whole deck heard his voice, before the great creature drew him down into the dark water, and he was gone. The crew stood frozen with horror for a moment, and then, at a cry from the captain, they began to fight again with double fury.

Another arm closed around Ned Land and began to crush him, and the harpooner struggled with his weapon, shouting with rage and pain. Nemo and Conseil hacked at the monster until it let go, and Ned fell to the deck, gasping and bruised, with his coat torn to rags. For the first time since the day of their capture, the Canadian looked at the captain with something very like gratitude in his eyes.

At last the surviving squid slipped back into the water and vanished into the deep, and the sea became calm again, as though nothing had ever happened. The deck was slippery with ink and with the dark blood of the monsters, and the men leaned on the rail, panting like runners at the end of a race. Nobody spoke, and nobody smiled, for every man there knew that the sea had taken one of their own that afternoon.

Nemo stood alone at the broken rail, looking at the place where his man had been taken, and the evening wind stirred his coat and his grey hair. Aronnax saw tears running down the cheeks of the captain, and he, who had thought him a man of iron, could find nothing to say. He stood a few steps behind him in silence, ashamed to disturb a grief that he had no right to share.

For days afterwards Nemo shut himself up in his cabin and would speak to nobody, and the whole crew moved through the ship in a heavy silence, as if the death of one man had stopped the clocks. Aronnax felt a deep pity for the captain, and he began to understand how heavy his sorrows were, and how much he carried alone. He wondered, as he sat alone in the salon that night, what the man had lost long before in the world above the waves.

The Nautilus followed the Gulf Stream, that great warm river which flows through the cold waters of the Atlantic like a living thing. Aronnax explained to his friends that it carries more water than all the rivers of the world together, and that its colour is a deep and brilliant blue. He had never seen so lovely a sight, and he thought it was like sailing through a vast and moving sapphire.

Ned Land told Aronnax in a low voice that the escape must be made when the ship was close to a coast, and that he had marked a place on the chart where the shore was near. He asked the professor to be ready on the first calm and misty night. Aronnax, who did not wish to refuse a friend, said that he would be, though his heart was heavy as he said it.

One morning a thick fog covered the sea, and the Nautilus came up to the surface to feel her way through the whiteness. Aronnax peered out from the deck into the mist and saw the dim shapes of ships far away, which loomed and vanished like ghosts. The sound of a distant bell reached him across the water, and he could not tell which ship had rung it in the fog.

A large warship with tall masts and black guns came slowly out of the fog, and she began to follow the Nautilus at a distance, as a dog follows a stranger. Aronnax could not see her flag, and Nemo, who stood at the window with his glass, said nothing at all. His face, in the grey light of the fog, was as pale and as hard as a mask carved from old stone.

The captain's face turned hard and cold in a way that the professor had never seen before, and his dark eyes burned with a terrible fire. He sent his three guests to their cabins and locked the doors himself, and then he returned to the window alone, with his hands clasped behind his back. Aronnax heard his steps go away along the passage, and then there was only the silence of the closed doors.

The warship fired upon the Nautilus, and Aronnax heard the shot strike the water close by, with a heavy sound like a falling tree. Nemo gave the order to dive and to turn the ship, so that she faced her enemy, and the Nautilus went down and round with an obedience that seemed almost eager. The professor sat on his bed in the locked cabin with his heart racing, and he listened to every sound of the ship.

The Nautilus drove forward under the water with all her power and struck the warship with her ram, and the old ship cracked open from side to side with a noise like thunder. The sea rushed in through the breach, and she began to sink at once, her masts leaning over and her guns slipping into the water. It all took only a few moments, and it was over before the professor had time to understand what was happening.

Aronnax was allowed to the window of the salon at last, and he saw the warship go down slowly with all her men, her masts leaning over towards the water. He turned away in horror, for he could not understand how the captain, whom he had seen weep for a drowned sailor, could do such a thing. The sea closed over the wreck, and nothing was left on the surface but a few broken pieces of wood and a little foam.

Aronnax went to the captain's cabin and found Nemo on his knees before a small portrait of a woman and two children, and the sight made the professor stop in the doorway as if he had been struck. The captain whispered a prayer and then cried out in a broken voice that it was enough, that it was enough. Aronnax did not dare to move or to speak, for he felt that he had walked in upon the most private grief of a man's life.

Nemo rose and turned, and he told the professor in a low and terrible voice that the nation of that ship had taken everything he had ever loved, and that he would never forgive it. Aronnax felt pity and horror struggle in his heart, but he could not forgive what he had seen. He decided that very night that he must leave the Nautilus and its terrible captain for ever, whatever it might cost him.

For days afterwards Nemo scarcely spoke and was scarcely seen, and the Nautilus drifted north through grey seas and gathering storms like a ship that had lost her course. The crew went about its duties in silence, with bowed heads, as if the whole vessel were in mourning for something that had no name. Aronnax thought that the captain's heart had been broken by his own terrible act, and that he now hated himself as much as he hated the world.

Aronnax told Ned and Conseil in a low voice, in the shelter of the library, that he had made up his mind to escape. Ned was overjoyed, and he declared that he had been waiting for this moment since the first day, and he gripped the professor's hand so hard that it hurt. Conseil, as always, said quietly that he would go wherever his master went, and he began to pack the few things that they owned.

The Nautilus drew near to the coast of Norway, and the sea grew rough and dark under a low and angry sky. A great storm rose around the ship, and the waves beat on her sides like fists, though the Nautilus felt no fear, for she was made for the deep and could ride out any weather. Aronnax felt the whole hull shudder beneath his feet, and he lay awake all that night listening to the roar of the water.

Late at night the three friends crept through the dark passages of the ship to the little boat, moving as softly as thieves in a house of sleepers. Ned Land began to loosen the bolts which held it in its hollow, and Conseil kept watch at the door, while Aronnax's heart beat so loudly that he feared the crew might hear. Not a single light shone in the long corridors of the ship, and not a single voice was heard on any side of them.

Suddenly a bell rang in the heart of the ship, and Aronnax heard the crew cry out the same word again and again in a language that he could not understand, and that he would never forget. He felt the whole vessel begin to turn on her axis, and he knew from the faces of his friends that something was terribly wrong. The great ship seemed to be falling, and the lamps swung wildly and went out, one after another, along the passage.

The Nautilus had been caught by the Maelström, that huge and terrible whirlpool which lies off the coast of Norway and which sailors have feared for centuries. The bolts gave way with a crash, and the small boat tore free of the hull, and spun like a toy round the edge of the whirlpool while the black water roared beneath. Aronnax closed his eyes and prayed for his friends and for the strange captain whom he was leaving to the sea.

The boat was thrown about like a leaf in a gale, and the foam hissed all around it in a white fury, so that the three men could see nothing. Aronnax was hurled against the side with great force and he lost his senses, and the world turned to black while the roaring of the sea filled his head. He did not know what happened after that, for the last thing he heard was the voice of the whirlpool, loud as a hundred storms.

When Aronnax woke, he was lying in a warm bed in the small hut of a fisherman, on one of the Lofoten Islands, and a soft grey light was falling through the little window. Ned Land and Conseil sat beside him, safe and unhurt, and the simple fishermen of the island were kind and asked them no questions. Aronnax pressed his friends' hands in silence, too full of thankfulness to say what he felt after so long and strange a journey.

As soon as he was strong again, Aronnax sat down at a table by the window and began to write the story of the voyage, putting down every sea, every wonder and every danger, so that nothing might be forgotten. He did not know what had happened to Captain Nemo and his ship, and he was not sure that he ever would. He only knew that the tale must be told, and that the world was owed a true account of the wonders and sorrows of the sea.

Aronnax closes his account with a wish that Captain Nemo has found peace at last, and that the hatred which made him a wanderer has finally faded from his heart. He hopes that the Nautilus is still crossing the oceans, with its great windows full of marvels, and that the sea, the only home Nemo ever loved, still shelters him. The learned world will decide whether his story is true, but he, Pierre Aronnax, knows that it is.
